LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD defines sources that are fetched from the project's official GitHub repository using HTTPS. The `source` array entries point to LICENSE and README files, as well as prebuilt binary archives for different architectures, all hosted under the legitimate upstream URL: `https://github.com/jpillora/cloud-torrent`. The source URLs are constructed dynamically but remain within the expected scope of the project's release assets and raw content.

Checksums are provided for all sources, including architecture-specific binaries, and none are set to 'SKIP'. The checksums are valid and match the expected format. There is no command substitution, `pkgver()` function, or top-level code execution outside of standard variable assignments. The `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` and `makepkg --printsrcinfo` commands will only fetch and verify these sources without executing any build or prepare functions, which are safely excluded by the flags used.

No evidence of malicious behavior is present in the global scope or source definitions. The file operations and network requests during this phase are limited to downloading verifiable, statically addressed assets over HTTPS, with no dynamic code evaluation or data exfiltration.
</details>
<evidence>

<summary>
No malicious code in sourcing or fetching.
</summary>
</security_assessment>

<details>
The PKGBUILD file defines a standard Arch Linux package build process for the `cloud-torrent-bin` package, which is a self-hosted torrent client. The source files are fetched from the official GitHub repository (`https://github.com/jpillora/cloud-torrent`) and its release assets, using versioned URLs (v0.9.4). The binary assets are downloaded as pre-built gzipped executables for multiple architectures, and appropriate SHA-256 checksums are provided for all sources, ensuring integrity verification.

The build process consists only of installing the pre-built binary, license, and README files into standard system directories (`/usr/bin`, `/usr/share/doc`, `/usr/share/licenses`). There are no suspicious commands, such as network access during build, use of `eval`, `base64` decoding, or execution of downloaded scripts. The package follows typical AUR practices for a `-bin` package, with no code compilation and proper use of checksums. No obfuscated or potentially harmful operations are present.

While the binary is distributed pre-compiled (common for `-bin` packages), the sources are from the project's legitimate release page, and checksums match expected values. This does not constitute a supply-chain attack, as there is no evidence of unauthorized modification, data exfiltration, or execution of unverified code during packaging.
</details>

</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for README-0.9.4.md:
<security_assessment>
<decision>UNSAFE</decision>
<details>
The README contains a highly suspicious and dangerous installation command that downloads and executes code directly from a URL using `curl | bash`. Specifically, the command `curl https://i.jpillora.com/cloud-torrent! | bash` retrieves a script from a domain controlled by the author and pipes it directly into `bash` for immediate execution without any verification or inspection.

This pattern is a well-known supply-chain attack vector, as it allows the remote server to deliver arbitrary, potentially malicious code to the user's system at any time. The use of a short URL (`i.jpillora.com`) further obscures the true source of the script, making it harder to audit. Even if the current script is benign, the lack of integrity checking and the ability for the remote party to modify the payload at any time makes this installation method inherently unsafe.

While the rest of the document describes legitimate project details, the presence of this installation method represents a clear security risk to end users and constitutes unsafe behavior in the context of software distribution.
</details>
<evidence>
curl https://i.jpillora.com/cloud-torrent! | bash
</evidence>
<summary>
Unsafe install command enables remote code execution</summary>
</security_assessment>
